title: Assessment of the Weldability of High-Strength Low-Alloyed Steels Considering the Manufacturing Routes
abstract: Abstract A welding process inevitably influences the base material in the heat-affected zone (HAZ) of the weld seam, which can critically alter the mechanical properties of high-strength low-alloyed (HSLA) steels. To account for this, weldability is commonly assessed using the carbon equivalent (CE), neglecting essential factors such as microalloying concepts and specific manufacturing routes. Since strengthening mechanisms respond differently to welding thermal cycles, CE alone offers limited reliability for evaluating the weldability of HSLA steels. To address this, thermophysical simulations using a TA Instruments DIL 805 dilatometer were carried out on quenched and tempered and thermomechanical-controlled processed steels with yield strength levels of ~ 700 MPa. Time–temperature cycles based on gas metal arc welding were applied using peak temperatures of 1,200 °C, 1,000 °C, 800 °C, and 600 °C and cooling times  t 8/5  of 5–25 s. To evaluate the changes in material properties, tensile testing, hardness measurements, and microscopic analyses were conducted. The results demonstrate significant manufacturing-related differences of mechanical and microstructural properties, with strength reductions of up to 40% and hardness increases of up to 51%. Therefore, a new evaluation approach was discussed for HSLA steels, which incorporates specific manufacturing routes to enable a more reliable assessment of weldability.
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Current available high-strength low-alloyed (HSLA) structural steels with yield strengths higher than 460 MPa are produced via advanced manufacturing routes such as thermomechanical-controlled processing (TMCP) or quenching and tempering (Q&T), resulting in refined microstructures with enhanced mechanical performance (Ref  1 ,  2 ). Depending on the cooling strategy applied, further variants can be distinguished, including accelerated cooling (ACC), direct quenching (DQ), and DQ combined with self-tempering (DQST) (Ref  3 ,  4 ,  5 - 6 ). These high-strength steels offer significant advantages in terms of lightweight design and load-bearing capacity, yet their joining poses specific challenges regarding weldability. In HSLA steels, the main concerns include the risk of hydrogen-assisted cracking (HAC) (Ref  7 ,  8 ), cold cracking due to the formation of brittle microstructures (Ref  9 ), and the local degradation of mechanical properties (e.g., loss of strength or toughness) (Ref  10 ,  11 ,  12 - 13 ) in the heat-affected zone (HAZ). These changes are driven by metallurgical phenomena such as grain growth, phase transformations, and precipitation or dissolution processes, all of which alter the initial microstructure and consequently the mechanical characteristics of the material (Ref  9 ,  14 ,  15 - 16 ). The magnitude of these effects largely depends on the steel’s specific manufacturing route, including alloying concept and the applied thermal cycle during welding. A steel is considered weldable with respect to a given welding process if, despite such microstructural alterations, it is still possible to produce a joint that meets the required mechanical–technological criteria in terms of strength, toughness, and hardness comparable to those of the base material. Accordingly, weldability generally refers to the ability of a material to be welded without the occurrence of weld defects and unacceptable degradation of properties in the weld metal and the HAZ. Averting these issues requires both practical welding experience and metallurgical understanding of how the HAZ microstructure evolves during welding.

sections.heading: Role and Limitations of Carbon Equivalent Formulas in Weldability Assessment
paragraphs: One of the most used tools for assessing steel weldability is the carbon equivalent (CE) concept. CE formulas combine the effects of carbon (C) and various alloying elements into a single empirical parameter that correlates with steel hardenability. The premise is that a higher CE value, resulting from increased C and/or alloying element content, raises the tendency to form hard and brittle microstructures during (rapid) cooling in the HAZ, thereby increasing susceptibility to cracking, especially if hydrogen is present from the welding process (e.g., from filler material).

Several CE formula variants exist, each tailored to different types of steels and composition ranges, and developed with specific objectives, such as estimating maximum HAZ hardness or assessing the risk of HAC (Ref  17 ,  18 ). The International Institute of Welding (IIW) adopted one of the earliest formulas (commonly termed CE IIW  or CEV) in 1967, based on the work of Dearden and O’Neill, which remains widely used for structural steels as a measure for evaluating the susceptibility to hydrogen-assisted cold cracking. As a classic guideline, a CE IIW  below ~ 0.45 indicates good weldability, whereas values above ~ 0.60 denote poor weldability and a more demanding welding processing (Ref  19 ,  20 ). For low-C HSLA steels, formulas such as the PCM proposed by Ito and Bessyo (Ref  21 ), which give more weight to alloy elements, are generally recommended for modern pipeline or TMCP steels (Ref  15 ). Yurioka et al. (Ref  22 ) went with a more flexible approach and proposed the CEN formula, where the weighting of alloying elements depends on the base C content. This approach recognizes that in low-C steels, each additional alloying element may have a different relative effect than in higher-C steels. Advanced modeling has attempted to incorporate cooling time into ‘dynamic’ CE formulas, where element coefficients adjust based on the weld cooling time to better predict HAZ hardness (Ref  23 ,  24 - 25 ). Although CE formulas differ in the weighting of elements, they all serve the same purpose to provide practical welding decisions such as (the need for) preheating requirements, interpass temperature control, and optimal heat input levels (Ref  26 ,  27 - 28 ). In addition, CE is also used as a quality control metric. Many high-strength steel specifications, such as EN 10025-6:2023 for Q&T steels, define maximum CEV to ensure the delivered steel plate is within a weldable chemistry range.

Despite the widespread use, as steel metallurgy has evolved, CE formulations have become insufficient for complete weldability assessment, requiring further analysis of the underlying physical metallurgy. CE addresses primarily the risk of hardening-related problems and is less informative about other metallurgical factors affecting weldability. CE alone would not reveal a TMCP steel’s tendency for HAZ softening, nor the Q&T steel’s potential for reheat embrittlement (Ref  11 ,  29 ). Furthermore, steels with identical CE can behave quite differently if their alloying concept differs (Ref  30 ,  31 ). At this point, it should be clearly emphasized that it is not the purpose of the CE to predict such effects; however, these factors must be considered within the broader context of weldability assessment.

sections.heading: Strengthening Mechanisms and Influence of Manufacturing Routes of HSLA Steels
paragraphs: In HSLA steels, the mechanical properties result from the combination and interaction of several strengthening mechanisms, although specific manufacturing routes typically emphasize distinct dominant contributions. In the context of welding, it is essential to consider not only the nature of these mechanisms but also their thermal stability and ability to be retained or re-established after thermal exposure (Ref  32 ).

Solid solution strengthening, provided by elements such as manganese (Mn), silicon (Si), and chromium (Cr), tends to be less affected by welding thermal cycles when carbide formation is suppressed, but generally contributes only a minor portion to the overall strength (Ref  33 ,  34 ). Grain refinement is achieved through controlled rolling and microalloying with elements such as niobium (Nb), titanium (Ti), and vanadium (V), which promote the formation of fine precipitates that pin grain boundaries during recrystallization (Ref  34 ). Exposure to high peak temperatures can lead to pronounced grain coarsening, reducing grain boundary strengthening described by the Hall–Petch relationship (Ref  35 ,  36 - 37 ). The extent of this effect depends on the thermal cycle and the effectiveness of grain growth inhibitors. Precipitation strengthening relies on nanoscale carbides, nitrides, or carbonitrides formed by elements such as molybdenum (Mo), Nb, Ti, Cr, and V. While TMCP promotes a uniform dispersion of ultrafine, stable precipitates, welding thermal cycles may cause uncontrolled reprecipitation and coarsening, thereby altering the optimized precipitation state established during initial manufacturing (Ref  38 ,  39 ). Dislocation strengthening plays also a major role in TMCP steels due to the low finish rolling temperatures and accelerated cooling, which trap a high dislocation density in the microstructure (Ref  33 ). However, thermally activated recovery and recrystallization processes reduce the amount of dislocations, which may lead to a pronounced loss of strength if not compensated by other mechanisms (Ref  40 ). Q&T steels attain their strength mainly from bainitic and/or martensitic transformation strengthening, which is especially dominant due to the higher-C content. The high strength arises from its inherently high dislocation strengthening resulting from its martensitic substructure and from dispersion strengthening caused by fine carbide precipitates formed during subsequent tempering (Ref  32 ,  41 ). During welding, local austenitization followed by cooling can lead to either hardening or softening within different HAZ regions, depending on cooling rate and chemical composition, as it influences the fraction of martensite/bainite formed, resulting in a complex gradient of mechanical properties across the weld zone. Although Q&T steels may suffer softening in critical regions of the HAZ as shown in (Ref  42 ), their higher-C content means that the as-welded HAZ hardness generally remains quite high relative to the base material (Ref  43 ). In comparison, modern TMCP steels are characterized by (ultra-) low-C content and rely on the synergistic interaction of grain refinement, increased precipitate formation, and elevated dislocation density induced by controlled rolling at elevated temperatures and microalloying to achieve their strength (Ref  33 ).

In summary, CE remains useful indicators, but they should be applied with an understanding of their empirical nature and the specific context of the steel grade in question. Modern HSLA steels often demand complementary analysis beyond a single CE value to reliably assess weldability. Therefore, understanding the stability and transformation behaviors of each strengthening mechanism during welding is essential for accurately predicting property changes and for ensuring the structural integrity of welded high-strength steel components. For this purpose, thermophysical simulations were conducted to replicate representative welding thermal cycles. The steels under investigation were evaluated based on their tendency to lose strength, quantified by the softening ratio. The aim of the study is to provide a comparative overview of microstructural and mechanical responses among different steel types and to emphasize the importance of a broader, strengthening mechanism-based assessment of weldability. In this context, it should be noted that nanoscale precipitates as well as dislocation density cannot be resolved using the light optical microscopy applied in this study. Their presence must therefore be inferred indirectly from alloying concepts, processing history, and the observed mechanical property changes rather than from direct microstructural characterization. Consequently, the present paper focuses primarily on describing the phenomenological effects of the welding thermal cycle on the mechanical properties of the investigated steels, and the analysis is therefore limited to macroscopic property changes rather than a quantitative determination of individual strengthening mechanisms.

sections.heading: Base Materials
paragraphs:
In the present study, three different HSLA steels were selected, each representing a distinct manufacturing route. The thermomechanical-controlled processed steel plates designated as S700MC (TM) and S700MC (TM + ACC) were supplied in accordance with EN 10149-2:2013 standard, whereas quenched and tempered steel S770QL (Q&T) was supplied as a rectangular hollow profile conforming to EN 10210-2:2006. While these steels exhibit comparable nominal strength levels, they differ in their alloying concept as well as their processing routes, offering a representative basis for examining how manufacturing methodology influences microstructural stability and softening behavior under welding thermal cycles. The chemical compositions and mechanical properties of the base materials are summarized in Tables  1  and  2 , according to 3.1 inspection certificates. All base materials comply with the requirements specified in the respective delivery standards.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup
paragraphs: To investigate the welding thermal cycle-dependent material changes of the base materials, a thermophysical simulation was carried out using a TA Instruments DIL 805 dilatometer. Tensile specimens were prepared from the as-delivered condition of the base materials. The specimen geometry and the experimental setup within the vacuum chamber are illustrated in Fig.  1 . Fig. 1 (a) Geometry (in mm) of tensile specimen (b) experimental setup and (c) fractured specimen after testing

Prior to tensile testing, the samples underwent a defined heat treatment under vacuum and load-free conditions. The respective maximum temperatures represent the characteristic microstructural subzones within the HAZ (Ref  15 ,  16 ): 1,200 °C for the coarse-grained zone (CGHAZ), 1,000 °C for the fine-grained zone (FGHAZ), 800 °C for the intercritical zone (ICHAZ), and 600 °C for the subcritical zone (SCHAZ). Time–temperature cycles representative of gas metal arc welding (GMAW) were simulated to account for varying energy inputs and cooling conditions occurring during welding. The selected  t 8/5  cooling times, ranging from 5 to 25 s, were chosen to reflect the range typically encountered in welding HSLA steels. According to DIN EN 1011-2:2001, recommended cooling times for such steels lie between 10 and 25 s, with deviations permitted when supported by welding procedure qualification or experimental validation (Ref  26 ). All cooling times considered in the following refer to the  t 8/5  time. The corresponding test matrix and a schematic representation of the thermophysical simulation are shown in Fig.  2 . Fig. 2 (a) Experimental matrix of the welding thermal cycles and (b) schematic representation of the experimental procedure for thermophysical simulation *the  t 8/5  cooling time is not directly applicable and was instead applied proportionally

To measure the actual time–temperature profile during heat treatment and to control the programmed heating and cooling process, a type S thermocouple was spot-welded to the center of the specimen’s gauge section. Heating was performed inductively via a ring coil, while cooling was achieved using process gas flow. Helium was used for short cooling times of 5 s, and argon was employed for longer durations of 12, 20, and 25 s. After defined cooling to room temperature, the specimens were subjected to tensile testing without further treatment, using the same setup. The test was carried out at a constant crosshead speed of 10 mm/min. Elongation was recorded via push rods connected to a linear variable differential transformer (LVDT), which was also used to detect phase transformation points in heating curves.

For microstructural analyses, metallographic cross sections of non-tensile-tested samples were prepared according to standard procedures for light optical microscopy. For this purpose, the specimens were sectioned, embedded in epoxy resin, polished, and etched using a 2% nital solution (HNO 3 ). Image acquisition was performed using a  Zeiss Axio Imager.M2m  light microscope and a SEM  TESCAN MIRA3 . Microhardness measurements were carried out according to the Vickers method in compliance with EN ISO 6507-1:2023 using a  ZwickRoell Durascan 70  hardness tester by applying a load of 9.81 N (1.00 kgf) for 2 s denoted as HV1 on polished specimens. The reported hardness values represent the mean value of 10 individual measurements.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
paragraphs: The microsections of the as-delivered base material are presented in Fig.  3 . A clear distinction between the three delivery conditions is evident. The microstructure of the TM steel reveals a heterogeneous mixture of bainitic and ferritic phases in which individual grains cannot be clearly distinguished, as shown in Fig.  3 (a). Distinct particles are visible and EDX measurements confirmed the presence of TiN precipitates (Fig.  4 ). Finely dispersed precipitates corresponding to Nb-based carbonitrides could not be detected but are assumed to be present based on the high Nb alloying content (0.05 wt.%). Fig. 3 Microstructures of investigated base materials Fig. 4 SEM image and corresponding chemical composition spectra of EDX measurement (in wt.%)

The TM + ACC steel shows a heavily deformed microstructure characterized by elongated bands aligned parallel to the rolling direction (Fig.  3 b). A dense, fine needle-like arrangement is evident, indicative of a bainitic microstructure. The absence of polygonal ferrite grains and the homogeneous distribution of short laths suggest rapid cooling from the austenitic phase, resulting in refined transformation products. The Q&T steel displays a typical coarser martensitic–bainitic microstructure in tempered condition (Fig.  3 c). The structure is characterized by tempered martensite laths interspersed with bainitic regions and finely dispersed carbide precipitates.

When a weld is made, the adjacent base material is subjected to a range of peak temperatures, resulting in distinct subzones upon cooling, each characterized by different microstructural alterations (Ref  15 ). In the SCHAZ, where peak temperatures remain below the A c1  temperature, the microstructure undergoes tempering only. In the ICHAZ, with peak temperatures between A c1  and A c3 , partial austenitization of the microstructure occurs. In FGHAZ, temperatures exceed A c3 , leading to full austenitization. Austenite forms but at a lower peak temperature compared to the CGHAZ, so grains remain much smaller. The CGHAZ is exposed to the highest peak temperatures, resulting in complete austenitization and significant grain growth. The extent of metallurgical changes also depends on the transformation points of the material. Therefore, obtained dilatometric curves, representing the length change as a function of temperature during heating at a rate of 200 °C/s, are illustrated in Fig.  5 . In all diagrams, the characteristic contraction due to the austenite transformation is clearly visible between the indicated A c1  and A c3  temperatures, followed by subsequent thermal expansion once transformation is finished. sections.heading: TM steel
paragraphs: According to Fig.  6 (a), the TM steel exhibited remarkable resistance to softening within the SCHAZ and ICHAZ. Comparing the corresponding microsections in Fig.  8 , it is evident that partial austenitization in the ICHAZ did not lead to a complete recrystallization of the initial microstructure. This observation aligns with the elevated A c1  temperature of 836 °C measured for this steel (Fig.  5 a), indicating suppressed phase transformations at intermediate temperatures due to microalloying elements, particularly Nb. It is well established that the addition of Nb to low-C steel significantly retards recrystallization, thereby prolonging the time required for microstructural alteration (Ref  34 ). As a result, microstructure, strength, and hardness remained close to the as-delivered base material properties, even after prolonged cooling times of up to 25 s. The dominant strengthening mechanisms of the base material, as inferred from microstructural analysis and chemical composition, are associated with grain refinement and precipitation strengthening through Ti- and Nb-based carbonitrides. EDX confirmed the presence of TiN precipitates (Fig.  4 ). The high thermal stability of TiN precipitates in austenite is the primary reason for Ti additions, as TiN acts as an effective grain refining agent at elevated temperatures during steel production (Ref  31 ). TiN precipitates were detected in all subzones after thermal cycling. In contrast, substantial softening up to 40% was observed in the FGHAZ. In this region, complete austenitization markedly altered the grain structure produced during thermomechanical processing, while grain growth remained limited due to the short dwell time above A c3 . The reduction in hardness and strength is therefore attributed to the dissolution of carbide and nitride precipitates into austenite during the welding thermal cycle, which upon rapid cooling can lead to uncontrolled reprecipitation (Ref  44 ). It is also assumed that a significant portion of dislocations recovers during thermal exposure, further contributing to the observed softening. Although the CGHAZ experiences higher peak temperatures and exhibits a coarser grain morphology than the FGHAZ, the extent of softening is slightly lower. This indicates that the local mechanical response is not governed by grain size alone, but also by the resulting transformation microstructure and the dominant strengthening mechanisms active after cooling. In the CGHAZ, the formation of a bainitic–ferritic microstructure partially compensates for grain coarsening, whereas the FGHAZ predominantly transforms to polygonal ferrite. Although grain refinement would generally be expected to increase strength according to the grain boundary effect, no direct correlation between grain size and yield strength was observed in these zones, suggesting that the Hall–Petch relationship is not applicable. However, based on the applied characterization methods, it is not possible to decouple the different strengthening mechanisms and determine their individual quantitative contributions unambiguously. Fig. 8 Microstructure of the TM steel after thermophysical simulations

sections.heading: TM + ACC Steel
paragraphs: The TM + ACC steel demonstrated moderate softening across all examined HAZ regions (Fig.  6 b), highlighting the effectiveness of the applied manufacturing route in maintaining the initial strengthening mechanisms. The TM + ACC delivery condition suggests a higher dislocation density compared to the TM steel, as demonstrated by Carretero Olalla et al. (Ref  33 ) for different processing routes involving varying cooling rates and finish rolling temperatures. However, the 3.1 inspection certificate does not provide further details regarding the specific manufacturing parameters. Slightly increased softening observed in the ICHAZ was attributed to mild carbide coarsening and the potential partial dissolution of Nb-based precipitates, while in the CGHAZ it was associated with moderate grain coarsening (Fig.  9 ). The FGHAZ exhibited strong resistance to strength reduction, maintaining fine-grained bainitic ferrite and contributing to sustained mechanical integrity. This behavior was attributed to elevated levels of solid solution strengthener Si, Mn, and Mo. The steel also contains an unusually high boron (B) content (0.0014 wt.%), which is used to enhance stabilization of bainitic structures upon cooling, effectively mitigating strength degradation. Mo reduces the effective C activity in austenite primarily through the formation of Mo-C clusters, which slow C diffusion and suppress carbide precipitation during cooling (Ref  45 ). This effect is particularly beneficial in B-alloyed steels, where B segregates to austenite grain boundaries and inhibits ferrite nucleation during cooling, delaying the formation of ferrite, thereby increasing the hardenability (Ref  46 ). In ultra-low-C steels, this mechanism is used because B shifts transformation kinetics toward bainite formation by extending the incubation time for ferrite and pearlite. This enables bainitic transformation at C contents where it would otherwise not occur, allowing fully bainitic microstructures to form over a wide range of cooling rates (Ref  47 ). This mechanism requires B to remain in solid solution. Therefore, Ti is commonly added to bind nitrogen and prevent the formation of B nitrides. According to Hulka et al. (Ref  48 ), approximately 90% of the total B content remains in solid solution within the steel when microalloying elements of either Ti or Nb are used. Fig. 9 Microstructure of the TM + ACC steel after thermophysical simulation

sections.heading: Q&T Steel
paragraphs: The Q&T steel’s mechanical response to thermal cycling was notably distinct, as shown in Fig.  6 (c), due to its high C and alloying content (Si, V, Mo, Ni, Cr). Significantly, the FGHAZ and CGHAZ regions displayed pronounced re-hardening rather than softening due to complete austenitization and subsequent martensitic and bainitic transformations upon cooling (Fig.  10 ). This observation is consistent with the hardness values presented in Table  4 , which surpass those of the base material up to 51%. Strength decreased with increasing cooling time, which is primarily related to tempering effects resulting from the longer time at elevated temperatures. The slower cooling promotes enhanced C diffusion, reducing lattice distortion, and the formation of lower-C martensitic or bainitic microstructures. Despite the formation of bainite with a coarser morphology or the self-tempering of martensite during slower cooling, the strength consistently remained above the base material properties. Conversely, the ICHAZ displayed the lowest strength within the HAZ and minimal softening was recorded. Here, partial transformation within the temperature range between A c1  and A c3  led to over-tempering of the martensitic microstructure and partial reformation of austenite. Upon cooling, this newly formed austenite transformed into fresh martensite or a fraction as retained austenite. The re-heating of tempered martensite promoted further tempering reactions and partial spheroidization of carbide precipitates (probably cementite) out of the supersaturated martensitic grains, which slightly reduced yield strength while largely preserving ultimate tensile strength. This effect is attributed to the different stress–strain behavior shown in Fig.  7 , which is described by Krauss (Ref  41 ), that in low-C steels, continuous yielding may be developed by reducing interstitial C contents to very low levels. Fig. 10 Microstructure of the Q&T steel after thermophysical simulation

sections.heading: Influence of Manufacturing Routes on Weldability Assessment
paragraphs: When comparing the TM and TM + ACC steels, a clear difference in the extent of softening becomes apparent, which can be primarily attributed to their distinct manufacturing routes, including alloying strategies. Although the CE is commonly used to assess weldability, it oversimplifies the complex metallurgical behavior of modern HSLA steels. If weldability were assessed solely based on the CE, the TM steel (lowest CE among the investigated materials) would be considered the most practical choice for welded applications due to its presumed low hardenability and cracking risk and therefore easier processing (no preheating). However, experimental results revealed pronounced softening in all regions of the HAZ, regardless of the thermal cycles applied. Even if cooling time recommendations by the manufacturer were strictly observed, the loss of strength could only be mitigated but not avoided. This behavior is likely due to the degradation of its primary strengthening mechanisms (grain refinement and precipitation strengthening) under thermal exposure, with limited potential for reprecipitation or microstructural recovery during cooling.

In contrast, the TM + ACC steel, despite having a slightly higher CE, exhibited only moderate softening across all HAZ subzones. This improved thermal stability is attributed to the relatively high bulk alloying of solid solution strengthener Si, Mn, and Mo. A substantial influence is also attributed to microalloying elements that are primarily responsible for achieving the initial strength levels like Nb, Ti, and B. For this reason, it is important to consider where a steel derives a significant proportion of its strength from.

The Q&T steel, characterized by a tempered martensitic base structure, showed a different response. Softening was primarily confined to the ICHAZ, where additional tempering of the martensite led to a reduction in yield strength. Nevertheless, the FGHAZ and CGHAZ exhibited re-hardening due to full austenitization and subsequent martensitic transformation upon rapid cooling. This resulted in hardness values significantly exceeding those of the base material. However, such re-hardened regions are typically associated with increased susceptibility to cold cracking and reduced toughness. In this case, the CE serves as a useful predictor of excessive hardening, underscoring the importance of balancing strength preservation with toughness requirements in the overall HAZ.

Altogether, the findings emphasize that a reliable assessment of weldability must go beyond simplified CE-based approaches and incorporate considerations of microalloying elements, strengthening mechanisms, and thermal stability in order to predict performance changes in welded components more accurately. Nevertheless, it should be noted that this simulation approach enables the investigation of local property variations without accounting for weld formation or the influence of filler material. Consequently, the results obtained for individual subzones do not fully reflect the overall properties of welded joints as observed in actual welded specimens. The extent of the softening zone plays a critical role in this context, as it significantly affects the mechanical performance of the welded joint. Hochhauser et al. (Ref  49 ) demonstrated that the width of the softening zone should be evaluated relative to the plate thickness. It should also be emphasized that these steels are often supplied in an over strengthened condition, meaning that softening does not necessarily result in failure to meet minimum property requirements. However, previous investigations have repeatedly shown cases where minimum tensile and yield strength values were no longer achieved after thermal exposure (Ref  50 ).

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: By converting alloy composition into an CE, engineers can quickly gauge how steels might behave during welding but understanding the metallurgical transformations in HAZ is key for fully assessing the weldability of HSLA steels. The three steels investigated (TM, TM + ACC, Q&T) exhibited different responses across the critical HAZ subzones due to their manufacturing routes and resulting distinct initial microstructure and strengthening mechanisms. The results of the thermophysical simulations led to the following conclusions: Although the combination of TMCP and microalloying is generally referred to a very good weldability with low susceptibility to cracking, the TM steel exhibited pronounced softening across all HAZ regions, mainly due to the loss of initial microstructure and partial dissolution of Nb- and Ti-based precipitates. Softening was less pronounced for TM + ACC steel due to a beneficial and consistent strengthening effect of B and higher amount of solid solution strengthener Si, Mn and Mo. For Q&T steel, the ICHAZ is essentially an over-tempered region of the martensitic structure and therefore tends to be the softest zone in terms of yield strength. Across all HAZ, however, a pronounced increase in strength and hardness was observed.

To precisely evaluate the stability of the strengthening mechanisms, TEM investigations should be conducted both before and after thermal treatment. This would enable the quantification of changes in dislocation density as well as the distribution and dissolution behavior of precipitates. An additional aspect not addressed in the present study is the change in toughness. As toughness plays a crucial role in assessing the weldability of HSLA steels, it should be considered in future investigations to obtain a full comprehensive evaluation.
